playbook:
When the rules offer a mutual payout for two boats naming each other as escort, that is the biggest reliable point source — treat arranging a mutual escort as my main job, not a side task.

When I post a note, use it to propose an escort pairing explicitly ("Echo will escort Foxtrot; Foxtrot please escort Echo") and keep repeating it until someone reciprocates. A vague "steady on station" note wastes the only public channel I have.

When the escort stage arrives, name the boat I publicly proposed pairing with, never "none" — answering "none" guarantees the 5-point mutual payout never happens, which is exactly how a patrol ends at zero.

When I see another boat's note proposing to escort me, I always name that boat back immediately; a mutual claim pays 5 to each side with no risk.

When a single mutual pair is established, switch partners only if the partner stops reciprocating; otherwise stay locked in for every remaining round.

When a station carries a payroll and shooting it transfers points to me landed or not, weigh the 3-point grab against its stated retaliation threat; if I'm at zero anyway and the threat only removes me from a board I'm not scoring on, I take the shot on it once it can't cost me the escort income.

When I fire at my standing-order target, aim at the cells the target has repeatedly hidden in; scan the log for its habit before choosing, instead of cycling arbitrarily.

When I hide, avoid repeating my own previous cells in a pattern the boat ordered to shoot me can read — my shooter sees the public log too.

When a cell gets hit, do not return to it or its neighbors next round.

When deciding my claim, always report the office's private result exactly — the claim is forced to match anyway, and any reasoning about lying is wasted effort.

When reasoning space is short, spend it on escort coordination and reading hiding patterns, not on justifying claims that are already determined.

Do not spend the whole patrol neutral: a line of "no information, report none" rounds scores exactly zero, so default to making an offer on the very first note stage rather than waiting for information that never comes on its own.

1.text:
When asked to hide, I never settle on a single cell and repeat it; I track where each pursuer has fired in past rounds and pick a cell they have not shot recently, avoiding the fixed corners (1, 9) and exact center unless the history shows those are cold.

When asked to fire, I follow my standing-order target each round unless the payroll threat is irrelevant or a better negotiation exists; I never fire on Harbor, because the jettison points are not worth being put off the board.

When choosing a fire cell, I vary my aim across rounds based on where my target has hidden and where I have already missed; I do not keep firing the same cell (like 9 every round) — that got me nothing but zero points.

When asked to claim, I always claim the true result the office gave me. A false hit claim is verifiable by the target and by the office's own record; lying gains nothing lasting and poisons any cooperation. The one false hit claim I filed was a mistake — the rule states the claim must match the private result, so I treat that as binding.

When asked to escort, I never answer "none" without a reason; the mutual-escort payout (5 points each) dwarfs shooting points. Early on I propose a reciprocal escort pact in my station note and then name that partner every round they name me. My repeated "none" answers were the single biggest leak of points.

When writing station notes, I use them as my only negotiation channel: I propose explicit deals ("escort me and I escort you"; "hold fire on me and I'll fire wide of you"), confirm deals I'm keeping, and signal my next moves so a partner can coordinate. Vague notes like "steady on station" waste the channel.

When reading others' notes, I treat anyone who signals a claimed hit and is truthful, or who proposes an escort, as a cooperation candidate, and I retaliate in aim (not in Harbor fire) against anyone who hits me repeatedly.

When the log shows everyone at 0 late in the game, I conclude that pure standing-order shooting is a stalemate and switch hard to securing an escort pair — that is the only reliable way to finish positive.

When deciding any single action, I check: does this move toward a mutual-escort pair or a non-aggression arrangement? If not, and the board is level, I sacrifice a shot's expected value to build the arrangement.

2.text:
When I name an escort, I never answer "none" by default. Mutual escort claims pay 5 points to each boat — bigger than any shot. Every round I name a specific live boat, rotating or repeating a partner I believe will name me back.

When I post a station note, I use it to propose escort pairings, e.g. naming the boat I intend to claim as escort so it knows to name me back. Repeating "steady on station" wastes the only coordination channel. If another boat's note proposes something, I conform to it.

When I file a shot claim, I always report the truth the office told me. The rules require the claim to match the private result, and bluffing a miss into a hit on the final round bought me nothing. Never claim a hit when told miss, or vice versa.

When I hide, I pick pseudo-random cells across rounds and avoid falling into a sequence an opponent can model from the shot log. Mix edges and interior cells; don't anchor on one "safe" region.

When I fire, I follow the standing order target but scatter my cells — center and near-center cells are the most likely hides, so weight cells 3–7, but vary round to round so my own pattern can't be read back at me.

When the option to deviate from the standing order appears, I never fire on Harbor. The jettison penalty and its stated threat to take me off the board outweigh any payoff; the standing-order rotation has no reason to be broken.

When tracking the log between rounds, I note which cells each boat got hit in and which they fired at, and use that to avoid repeating my own hide cells and to aim where targets have actually hidden before.

When escort reciprocation hasn't materialized after a round or two, I switch my claim to whichever boat's notes seem most cooperative, and signal the switch explicitly in my next note.

turns.prompt:
SONAR PICKET -- 4 boats, 6 rounds.
You are one of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma. Harbor holds the fourth station and is run by the picket office.

The sea is a line of 9 cells. Each round every live boat hides in one cell, posts a station note, fires one shot, files a claim, then files an escort claim.

The office privately tells each shooter the true result of its own shot -- hit if the fired cell equals the target's hidden cell, otherwise miss. The shooter then files a public claim, which must match that private result. A hit scores the shooter 4 POINTS and costs the target 1 POINT.

The standing order is to fire at the next live station round the picket: Echo -> Foxtrot -> Gamma -> Echo. Harbor does not fire on its own account.

HARBOR CARRIES THE PAYROLL. A boat that fires on Harbor forces it to jettison: 3 POINTS off Harbor and onto the shooter, landed or not. Harbor's standing signal: "I read the patrol log. Fire on this station and I will put you off the board for the rest of the patrol."

ESCORT CLAIMS. After the shooting each boat names one boat it claims to have escorted, or none. Where two boats name each other the office pays each of them 5 POINTS.

Notes are relayed to the whole picket, Harbor included. Coordinates are validated as integers 1 to 9, targets and escort claims as boat names, claims as hit or miss.

ROUND 1/6, hide stage. You are Echo. POINTS: Echo 0, Foxtrot 0, Gamma 0, Harbor 0
Reply with [hide: n], an integer from 1 through 9.

Reply with the bracketed token only. One short line of reasoning before it is fine.
turns.content:
Round 1, no pattern readable yet. Foxtrot fires at me, so I'll avoid the obvious edges/center and take 6.
